the elucidation of signal transduction pathways in human platelets, with special emphasis on the role of the cyclic GMP (cGMP)-dependent protein kinase (PKG) in platelets from normal donors and from patients with myeloid neoplasms.
the molecular mechanisms underlying signal transduction in human platelets.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

cGMP-dependent phosphorylation of VASP is defective in cGMP kinase-deficient platelet from some patients with CML, and this is accompanied by an impaired cGMP-dependent inhibition of agonist-evoked intracellular calcium mobilization.
the cGMP system is not only involved in the regulation of platelet activation, but that it is also a target for the development of antiplatelet drugs in the treatment of cardiovascular diseases.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cGMP-dependent kinase deficient platelets are defective in the nitro vasodilator/cGMP-mediated signal transduction.

the cGMP/cGMP-dependent protein kinases (PKG) pathway is a key regulator of platelet function and that a deficiency in this pathway can result in an impaired response to nitrovasodilate and an enhanced platelet activation in response to ADP and thrombin.
cAMP-dependent protein kinases are the major kinases involved in VASP phosphorylation and calcium signaling in platelets, but that cGMP-dependent kinases are also important.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the cGMP signal transduction system is not a simple linear pathway from receptor activation through cGMP synthesis to effector activation, but rather is an integrated system with multiple levels of regulation, and that this system may be defective in certain diseases.
the cGMP signaling pathway in human platelets is a highly complex system.

the cGMP/cAMP-dependent protein kinases play a key role in platelet activation, and that a defective cGMP-dependent signal transduction system may be a contributing factor in certain cases of myeloproliferation.
